Welcome!

text:
Tendon training is the missing piece of strength: muscle doesn’t touch the bone, tendons do, and they set the ceiling on how much of your strength you can actually use. Here are 5 no-equipment tendon exercises you can do in under 5 minutes.

▶Feel ten years younger👉 https://greyguyfitness.com/

In this video:

Dead hang: stronger forearms, elbows and shoulders
Wall sit: slow, steady tension for the tendons around your knee
Eccentric heel drop: the Achilles tendon, explained with the research
Isometric push-up hold: the push side of your upper body
Glute bridge hold: the tendons behind your hips and knees

Every move is a long hold or a slow lowering phase instead of a fast rep, because tendons adapt more slowly than muscle. You’ll also learn the doses, the progressions, and the mistakes to avoid, plus what the grip strength research really does and doesn’t tell us.

No gym, no barbell, no machine. Train 3 times a week and your tendons start catching up with your muscles.

👍 Subscribe for the next video.

FREE: Find your real body age in 60 seconds, then turn back the clock in 7 days (40+) 👉 https://grey-guy.kit.com/bodyage

To combine cardio and strength in one move: Check out these ropeless jump ropes 👉 https://www.Crossrope.com/GREYGUY

---------------------------------------------------------------- 

STUDIES & SOURCES MENTIONED IN THIS VIDEO:

• Grip Strength & Mortality Risk (PURE Study):
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/la...
A massive study showing hand grip strength is a stronger predictor of overall longevity and heart health than blood pressure.

• Isometric Exercises & Blood Pressure (Sports Medicine Review):
https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/57/20/1317
A major review demonstrating that static holds like wall sits lower resting blood pressure better than traditional cardio or weightlifting.

• The Alfredson Achilles Protocol (Original 1998 Study):
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.id/9702271/
The landmark clinical trial proving that heavy eccentric heel drops heal chronic Achilles tendon pain without surgery.

• 5-Year Achilles Follow-Up Study:
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.id/15088926/
Long-term data showing that people who completed the 12-week heel drop protocol kept their pain reduction and tendon function 5 years later.

• Biology of Tendon Aging & Healing (2023 IJMS Review):
https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/24/3/2633
An in-depth scientific review detailing how tendons lose stem cells and blood flow as we age, making them much slower to heal than muscles.

---------------------------------------------------------------- 

FURTHER READING ON TENDON TRAINING:

This study reveals that tendons adapt and gain stiffness much more slowly during strength training than muscles do—and lose those gains faster when you stop training. 

Keitaro Kubo 1, Toshihiro Ikebukuro, Hideaki Yata, Naoya Tsunoda, Hiroaki Kanehisa (2010) Time course of changes in muscle and tendon properties during strength training and detraining: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19996...
DOI: 10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181c865e2

#DumbbellWorkout #VTaper #BackWorkoutSearch Keywords

Build a wider back, broader shoulders, and a stronger V-shaped physique with these 5 dumbbell exercises — no gym or pull-up bar needed.

In this workout, you'll discover five uncommon dumbbell movements designed to target the muscles that contribute most to a powerful V-Taper: the lats, side and rear delts, upper back, traps, and shoulder stabilizers.

These exercises can be performed with dumbbells and simple home equipment, making them a powerful addition to your home muscle-building routine.

Focus on controlled repetitions, proper technique, and gradually increasing the challenge over time.

text:
Not medical advice: we're not doctors or trainers. Under 18? Keep efforts moderate. Stop if anything hurts.

REP THEORY 90, the full 90-day plan written out week by week 
(every week, every set, every hold + a 90-day tracker): https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/rt90

Have you ever noticed some skinny guys are way stronger than their size? It's their tendons. Here's how to train yours at home without getting bulky: 4 holds, the one rule that decides whether tendon training works, a simple wall-hold test, and a 12-week plan. If you watched "How Some Skinny Guys Are Stronger Than Big Guys", this is how you train it.

🔗 Free home plans and self-tests: https://www.reptheory.online/
🤝 Train with the community on Telegram: https://t.me/thereptheory

Chapters
00:00 - Why some skinny guys are so strong
00:35 - Hold 1: the wall hold (and the test)
01:52 - Hold 2: the heavy calf hold
02:59 - Hold 3: push something that won't move
04:03 - Hold 4: the hang
04:58 - The rule (hold long, hold heavy)
06:16 - The whole plan
07:17 - Your wall hold result
07:52 - Join the community

Research mentioned: Kubo et al. 2001 (J Appl Physiol: 12 weeks of 20-second isometric holds made tendons 57% stiffer, strength +34%, muscle volume +8%); Kubo et al. 2001 (J Physiol: same total work, only the 20-second holds stiffened the tendon, not 1-second contractions); Arampatzis et al. 2007 (J Exp Biol: only high tendon strain made the Achilles stiffer and thicker); Bohm et al. 2015 (Sports Med Open: meta-analysis of 27 studies, loading intensity matters most); Moritani & deVries 1979 (Am J Phys Med: early strength gains are mostly neural). The wall-hold tiers are our own simple scale, not a medical or fitness assessment.

Image (Wikimedia Commons, public domain): "Rectus femoris", Gray's Anatomy plate modified by Uwe Gille, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Fi...

Disclaimer: We are not doctors, physical therapists, dietitians, certified trainers or any other licensed health or fitness professionals. This video is for education and entertainment, based on the published research listed above, and is not personal medical, training or nutrition advice. Isometric holds raise blood pressure: breathe through every hold, and check with a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, a heart condition or a joint injury. Make sure any door frame, bar or step you use is solid. Stop if you feel sharp joint pain. If you're under 18, keep the effort medium and skip extra weight.

In 1988, Naim Süleymanoğlu, the weightlifter they called Pocket Hercules, weighed about 60 kg and lifted 190 kg over his head. That is more than three times his own body weight. This video breaks down the three hidden reasons behind that kind of strength: the physics of a light frame, the wiring of your nervous system, and your tendons, the steel cables that carry every bit of force your muscles make. Then you get a 12 week home plan to train them with no weights at all.

• Why smaller bodies are stronger pound for pound (the square cube law)
• How your brain decides how much of your muscle you can actually use

• Why endless easy push ups build muscle but leave your tendons behind
• Why heavy loading changes tendons and light training barely does
• Why teenagers need to build tendon strength before ramping up training

text:
TENDON THEORY, 12 weeks of holds written out (every hold, how long, how heavy, when to go up; the bar hang and a doorframe row hold for your elbows): https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/te...


A bodybuilder twice his size can't do five pull-ups. The skinny guy next to him does twenty. The difference isn't muscle. In the research, pull-ups had almost nothing to do with maximum pulling strength and a lot to do with strength for your own body weight. And every pull-up hangs your whole body off a few cables: the tendons in your fingers, your elbows and your shoulders.

Three holds that train those cables, one slow rep that ties them together, and a plan to go from a few pull-ups to a lot. No equipment beyond a bar and a chair.

What's in the video:
• The hang test: arms straight, shoulders pulled down, hang as long as you can. Your number tells you where to start.
• Why tendons matter: twelve weeks of hard 20-second holds made tendons 57% stiffer. Quick reps built the same strength, but only the holds made the tendons stiffer.
• Stiff vs loose: a loose tendon is a bungee cord, the bar moves late. A stiff one is a chain.
• Why elbows get sore: muscles get stronger faster than tendons. The muscle is ready, the cable isn't.
• Hold 1, the bar hang: 3 × 30 to 45 seconds at about 7 out of 10 effort. Longer than 45? Go heavier with a backpack, not longer.
• Hold 2, the shoulder-blade hold: 5 × 5 seconds, the first inch of every pull-up.
• Hold 3, the three-angle hold: top, halfway and near-straight arms, 5 seconds each, 3 rounds.
• The slow rep: the 5-second negative, 5 reps. Can't do 5 seconds yet? Start with 3 and add one a week.
• The plan: small clean sets (can do 6? do 4s), one rep more a week, stop with 1 or 2 reps left, three days a week, think twelve weeks, not two.
• Your hang test result: under 30 s → the bar hang and the slow reps first · 30 to 60 s → the whole plan · 60 to 90 s → add the backpack · over 90 s → weighted top and halfway holds.

Tendons aren't the whole story: your weight and practice matter too. They're just the part almost nobody trains on purpose.

Comment your hang-test time, and retest in four weeks.

Safety first: we're not licensed professionals, so train at your own risk. Hard is fine, painful isn't: if anything gives you sharp pain, stop, and if it doesn't go away, see a licensed physician right away. This video is general information, not medical advice. Results depend on where you start. The holds, times, plan and test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

text:
REP THEORY 90, the 90-day plan on sale right now: https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/rt90

If you can do five push-ups, you can do a handstand. I'll prove it. A handstand isn't held up by your shoulders, it's steered by your fingers: in the research, more than three quarters of the balancing came from the wrists. We follow Day 1 from his first second upside down to his first handstand, through six steps. Every step has a number to hit before you earn the next one.

A handstand for beginners progression at home with no equipment, from zero to your first 2-second freestanding hold. Built for skinny guys: the lighter you are, the less your fingers have to catch.

What's in the video:
• The pike test: hands down, hips up, shoulders over your hands, and count the seconds. Your result at the end tells you which step you start on.
• How a handstand really works: your palm carries your weight, your fingers steer. Gymnasts correct a wobble in about a fifth of a second, and the wrist flexors work harder than any other muscle.
• Why skinny guys have the edge: the work your fingers do to catch the same wobble grows with your body weight.
• Step 1, finger presses: 3 sets of 10. Shift your shoulders past your hands and press your fingertips into the floor.
• Step 2, the straight line: the overhead reach check, then a 30-second hollow hold with your lower back flat.
• Step 3, the chair pike: 30 seconds, arms locked, pushing tall. Your shoulders' real job.
• Step 4, chest to the wall: 30 seconds, hands one hand-length from the wall.
• Step 5, the bail: the cartwheel bail, 10 each side, from almost straight upside down. The step almost nobody practises.
• Step 6, leave the wall: float your toes off by one centimetre, then 2 seconds with nothing touching but your hands.
• Why most people fall in the first second: the wrong shape, looking at your feet, and late corrections.
• From two seconds to ten: the soft kick-up.
• How to train it: about 10 minutes most days, your current step plus the one before it, stop when the holds get shaky.
• Your pike test result: under 10 s → step 1 · 10–29 s → step 2 · 30–59 s → step 3 · a minute or more → step 4.

Comment your pike-test number and the step you're starting on.

Safety first: we're not licensed professionals, so train at your own risk. Warm up your wrists every session. Being upside down raises the pressure in your eyes, so breathe, don't strain, and come down if you get dizzy. If anything causes pain, stop and see a licensed physician right away. This video is general information, not medical advice. The step numbers and the test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

Keep losing arm wrestling matches at school to the big guy who slams his elbow on the desk? Here's how to win at arm wrestling even if you're skinny, using technique instead of size.

Arm wrestling isn't decided by the bigger arm. It's decided by the hand. Whoever controls the hand and the wrist controls the lever, and once his wrist bends back, most of his strength never reaches you. With the right setup, grip and timing, a skinny guy can beat a bigger, stronger opponent at the school desk, and do it without getting hurt.

What you will learn:
• Why arm wrestling is decided by the hand and the wrist, not the size of your biceps
• The setup that wins before anyone says go: foot forward, hip to the table, elbow tucked, knuckles high, wrist straight
• What to do on go against a stronger guy, how to wait him out, and when to hit the top roll
• When to switch to the hook, and why it's only for an even match
• How to finish with your shoulder and body weight, not your arm alone
• The position behind most broken arms in arm wrestling, and how to stay out of it
• 3 wrist exercises you can do at home with a hammer and a backpack

text:
TENDON THEORY: the 12-week plan that trains every tendon, not just your arm → https://gum.co/u/o8e5ailx

Want to beat bigger guys at arm wrestling? Train your tendons. In an arm wrestle, late loses. Your hand-closing muscles sit in your forearm, and their force reaches your fingers through tendons, so stiff tendons get it there first. This video covers the four moments every match comes down to (the go, the wrist, the squeeze and the line), the four home moves that train each one, a 20-minute plan, and the cup test to see where you start.

Safety first: keep your hand in front of your shoulder and in line with your elbow, never turn away from your arm, warm up first, and if you're beaten, let go. Under 18? Keep every hold at about 7/10, never all-out. This video is general information, not medical advice. The cup-test times are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

text:
Doing push-ups every day and your shoulders still look narrow? Push-ups mostly train the front of your shoulder. What makes you look wide is the side, and a push-up never works it the way it grows.

Your shoulder has three parts: a front, a side and a back. This video shows how to grow the side with a side raise done the way a study of competitive bodybuilders found works it hardest, why you can mostly skip front raises if you already do push-ups, and how to build the back of your shoulder at home with nothing but a sturdy table. Then the three things that decide whether any of it works, and a simple plan.

What you will learn:
• Why push-ups don't make your shoulders wider
• Why every centimetre on the side of your shoulder counts twice
• The three side-raise fixes: near-straight arms, thumbs forward, no shrugging
• Why water jugs or a backpack of books work as well as dumbbells, and why you don't need a cable machine
• Why front raises mostly repeat work your push-ups already do
• The wide table row: the home exercise for the back of your shoulders, with an easier and a harder version
• Hard sets, adding reps before weight, and the food that builds width
• A two-to-three-day plan and a tape-measure test for 12 weeks

Navy SEAL Bodyweight Exercises: 5 Proven Movements to Defy Aging After 40

Discover the exact bodyweight exercises Navy SEALs use to maintain peak performance well into their 50s. These five functional strength movements build capability without destroying your joints—no gym or equipment required.

What You'll Learn:
Navy SEALs train for decades without their bodies breaking down, and in this video, I reveal their complete bodyweight training system. Learn the dead hang technique that predicts longevity better than any other metric, the bear crawl pattern that builds bulletproof shoulders, and three other essential exercises that target the movement patterns and stability systems that actually keep you moving as you age.

The 5 SEAL-Proven Exercises:
Dead Hang - Build grip strength and decompress your spine 
Bear Crawl - Develop core stability and shoulder strength
Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift - Fix muscle imbalances and prevent back pain 
Pike Push-Up - Build overhead pressing power without joint stress 
Hollow Body Hold - Create anti-extension core strength 

Why These Exercises Work After 40:
Unlike traditional gym routines that focus on muscle size and often lead to joint damage, these bodyweight movements target functional strength and stability. Military research proves this training prevents shoulder impingement, fixes anterior pelvic tilt, strengthens rotator cuffs, and builds the deep stabilizer muscles regular exercises completely miss.
Perfect for men over 40 who want to maintain strength, mobility, and independence without gym memberships or equipment. Each exercise includes proper form cues, weekly progression plans, and safety modifications for existing shoulder or knee issues.

Your 3-Day Weekly Routine:
Follow the simple Monday-Wednesday-Friday plan outlined in the video. Start with one set of each exercise, master the positions in week one, then progressively add time and reps. Complete workouts take just 15-20 minutes.

5 Dumbbell Exercises That Build a THICK Neck Faster Than Shrugs

#NeckWorkout #ThickNeck #NeckExercises #DumbbellWorkout #DumbbellExercises #NeckTraining #BuildMuscle #UpperTraps #StrengthTraining #PhantomCore

Want to build a thicker, stronger-looking neck instead of relying only on shrugs? In this video, you'll learn 5 dumbbell exercises that train different functions of the neck while also developing the upper traps that create a powerful transition into your shoulders.

We break down Prone Dumbbell Neck Extensions, Lying Dumbbell Neck Flexion, Side-Lying Dumbbell Neck Flexion, Dumbbell Neck Isometric Holds, and Dumbbell High Pulls — including proper technique, sets, reps, and common mistakes to avoid.

In this workout you'll learn how to:

Train the front, back, and sides of your neck

Build neck strength with controlled dumbbell resistance

Use isometric resistance for neck stability

Develop the upper traps around the base of the neck

Progress safely without unnecessary heavy loading

Direct neck training should start conservatively. Use very light resistance, controlled ranges of motion, and secure padding/support whenever a dumbbell is positioned against the head. Stop if you experience pain, dizziness, numbness, or unusual symptoms, and seek professional guidance if you have an existing neck or spine issue.

If you want a physique that looks powerful from your shoulders all the way to your head, don't train only what you see in the mirror.

text:
REP THEORY 90: the 90-day plan with the push-up base and the planche lean built in → https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/rt90

If you can hold a plank for 30 seconds, you can do a planche. I'll prove it. A planche isn't a strength trick, it's a lever: your hands are the pivot, your body is the bar, and the further your weight sits from your hands, the heavier you get. Shorten the bar, and your body can hold it. We follow Day 1 from his first face-plant to his first planche, through seven links. Every link has a number to hit before you earn the next one.

What's in the video:
• The fingertip test: lean in a push-up position until your shoulders are over your fingertips and count the seconds. Your result at the end tells you which link you start on.
• Why skinny guys have the edge: the load in a planche is your weight times its distance from your hands, and strength only rises with about the two-thirds power of body weight. Bigger people are stronger, but not as much stronger as they are heavier. That's why elite ring gymnasts average about 167 cm and 65 kg (and no, gymnastics doesn't make you short).
• Link 1, the push-away plank: push the floor away and spread your shoulder blades. That's the serratus, the planche's secret muscle. Goal: 30 seconds.
• Link 2, the planche lean: a knee push-up puts about half your weight on your hands, a push-up about two-thirds, a planche all of it. Lean one finger-width further each week. Goal: shoulders over your fingertips, 3 holds of 15 seconds.
• Link 3, the frog stand: your feet leave the floor for the first time (put a pillow in front of your face). Goal: 30 seconds.
• Link 4, the tendons: straight arms load the tendon at the front of your elbow and your wrists. Muscles adapt in weeks, tendons in months: in one study, strength was up about 30% after two months of holds, but the tendons only caught up in month three. About half of young gymnasts report wrist pain. Three rules: wrists first, one change a week, pain means stop.
• Link 5, the lift-off: straight arms, round your back, lift your feet for a moment. Push-up handles, parallettes or two stacks of books work. Goal: 6 lift-offs of 2 seconds. Why the best planche drill is the planche itself.
• Link 6, the tuck planche: knees tucked, arms locked, nothing touching but your hands. Goal: 10 seconds. That's your first planche.
• The 3 ways people fake the tuck: bent elbows, not leaning far enough, and pinching the shoulder blades.
• Link 7, the road to the full planche: advanced tuck, one leg out, straddle, full. The honest timeline: a tuck takes most people a few months, a full planche a year or two.
• Train it like a skill: why four short sessions beat one brutal one, and why your tendons need the day in between.
• The plan: 4 days a week, about 15 minutes. 2 minutes of wrists, 5 holds of your current link, 2 easy sets of the link before it, 3 sets of push-ups. Move up after two clean sessions in a row.
• Your fingertip test result: under 5 s → link 1 · 5–14 s → link 2 · 15 s+ → link 3 · 30 s and easy → respect link 4.

Comment your fingertip-test number and your link, and reply the day you hold your first tuck planche.

Safety first: warm up your wrists every session, lean only as far as you can hold with straight arms, and stop on any sharp wrist or elbow pain. Under 18? Your tendons are still catching up with your muscles, so keep the holds short and stay on each link longer. This video is general information, not medical advice. The link numbers and the test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

These 5 Dumbbell Exercises Build MONSTER TRAPS Faster Than Shrugs

#TrapWorkout #MonsterTraps #DumbbellWorkout #Traps #TrapExercises #DumbbellExercises #BiggerTraps #UpperBackWorkout #BuildMuscle #PhantomCore

Want to build bigger, thicker traps with dumbbells? These 5 dumbbell exercises challenge your trapezius through more than just traditional shrugging, helping you train your upper back with different loading, arm positions, and scapular movements.

Shrugs can be an effective upper-trap exercise, but your trapezius is a large muscle with upper, middle, and lower regions that contribute to different movements of the shoulder blades. In this workout, we use five different dumbbell exercises to create a more complete approach to trap training.

5 Dumbbell Exercises:

Dumbbell Farmer’s Carry
Prone Dumbbell T-Raise
Incline Dumbbell Y-Raise
Chest-Supported Dumbbell Scapular Row
Dumbbell Prone W-Raise

The goal isn’t to perform five different versions of a shrug. Farmer’s carries challenge loaded stability, while T-Raises, Y-Raises, scapular rows, and W-Raises challenge your upper back through different positions and movement patterns.

Use controlled technique, choose appropriate resistance, and progress gradually. Bigger traps are built over time through consistent training, progressive overload, sufficient recovery, and proper nutrition.

text:
Ever noticed how some skinny guys can push, pull or hold things a much bigger guy can't move? It's not muscle. It's isometrics, training by holding still. 
This is the full guide: by the end, you'll know everything you need to start isometric training at home, with no weights.

🧱 Free home plans and self-tests: https://www.reptheory.online/

🤝 Train with the free community on Telegram: https://t.me/thereptheory

What's inside:
• Why holding still works: your muscles produce more force holding still than when they're lifting, and your brain learns to fire everything at once.

• Hold 1, the bottom of a push up: your strength test. The "push the floor away" cue, what 10, 20 and 30 seconds feel like, the sagging-hips mistake, and how to make it easier or harder.

• Hold 2, the deep split squat: why isometric strength is angle specific, why the bottom position carries over best to real movements, and the mistake of drifting up when you get tired.

• Hold 3, overcoming isometrics: pushing or pulling something that won't move (a towel curl, a palm press, a door frame), going from zero to everything in an instant, and how to breathe through it.

• Hold 4, the hollow body hold: the position gymnasts build almost everything on, the lower-back cue, and the beginner version.

• Hold 5, the wall handstand: how to walk up the wall, the "push the floor away" cue, the banana-back mistake, and the pike hold if you're not ready yet.

• Hold 6, the L sit: from the tuck L sit on two chairs to a full L sit, plus the feet-down version everyone starts with.

• The rule: the "two dials" (long holds at 7 out of 10, short all-out pushes) and three mistakes that waste your holds.

• Questions everyone asks: can holds replace weights? Will they make you bulky? Can you do them every day? How long should each hold be? Why do your muscles shake? Plus the blood pressure finding nobody expects.

• A full week you can copy: Monday, Wednesday and Friday sessions of about 15 minutes, a 5-minute version for busy days, and what to expect over 12 weeks.

• Your test result: what your push-up hold time means and which hold to start with.

If you watched "How Training Tendons Makes You Stronger Than Big Guys", this is the next step.

Research mentioned: Oranchuk et al. 2019 (Scand J Med Sci Sports: review of 26 studies; holds at long muscle lengths built more muscle, explosive intent built faster force, tendons need 70%+ effort); Lum & Barbosa 2019 (Int J Sports Med: isometric strength is angle specific; how to hold for size and for maximum strength); Edwards et al. 2023 (Br J Sports Med: a review of 270 trials; isometric training lowered resting blood pressure the most of the exercise types tested); the force-velocity relationship (muscles produce more force holding still than while lifting); Moritani & deVries 1979 (early strength gains are mostly neural). Make sure any chair, wall or bar you use is solid and the space around you is clear. Stop if you feel sharp joint pain.
